Hendersonville.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Hendersonville in Henderson County, where southern Blue Ridge mountains south of Asheville puts woods and water right against housing. Raccoons den in chimneys and attics in spring, squirrels chew soffits year-round, and bats use older rooflines in summer.

Most Hendersonville jobs start with a full roofline, attic, and crawlspace inspection, then removal and sealing as one job, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Hendersonville sits a thousand feet below Asheville in the mild valley of the French Broad, and the difference shows in the work. This is apple country — orchards across the county's rolling ground — and a historic small city of brick downtown streets, older neighbourhoods under mature oaks, and a large retiree population in homes that season quietly. The wildlife follows the valley's terms: raccoons and gray squirrels in the older homes near downtown, groundhogs in the orchard banks and garden edges, skunks under the porches, and bats in the tall attics of the Victorian-era stock that Hendersonville kept and Asheville's hills never had room for.

The retiree pattern shapes the second half of the call log. Hendersonville homes sit empty for stretches — winters in Florida, summers elsewhere — and a quiet house in the valley is claimed the same way it is everywhere: bats in the attic by spring, a raccoon in the chimney by the following one. Our Hendersonville inspections are built for owners who may not be in the house when they call us: full documentation, photographs of every entry and every seal, and a report that reads clearly from five hundred miles away.
Hendersonville.extendedBody:
Orchard-edge and valley work

Henderson County's orchards feed its wildlife as reliably as its people. Groundhogs hold the sunny banks between the orchard rows and the roads, denning where the mowing stops; raccoons work the fruit ground in season and the attics out of it; coyotes are heard across the valley at night. Properties at the orchard edge get an inspection weighted to the ground line — burrows at the banks and outbuildings, fence-line runs, and the garden-edge dens — beside the standard roofline read. The valley floor also collects water: the French Broad's bottoms and the creeks crossing the county bring beaver work to the low properties, dams in the drainage that back water toward yards and drives.

Credentialed work, and the bat calendar

Our Hendersonville operators are licensed Wildlife Control Agents with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission, working under the state's depredation-permit system — the permit issued for your property is the legal basis of the removal, and it sets what may be done with each species. Bats carry a hard calendar in North Carolina: evictions are prohibited during pup season, May 1 through July 31. Hendersonville's older homes hold little brown and big brown bat colonies in their tall attics; a colony found in the window is mapped and staged, then excluded completely in August, every gap sealed, because valley attics are re-let to bats the following spring if one entry survives.

The empty-house problem, handled on paper

For seasonal owners we run a pre-departure seal: the whole roofline and chimney inspected while you are in residence, residents excluded, entries closed in metal — and a written, photographed record of it all. The houses that stay empty of animals are the ones sealed to be empty; the report is how you verify it from wherever winter takes you.
